title: Grade 7 World History: Medieval to Early Modern

learn: In 330 CE, Emperor Constantine moved the Roman capital to Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople.
Its location between Europe and Asia made it a centre of trade.
The eastern Roman Empire, called the Byzantine Empire, lasted until 1453.
lessons.try: Locate Constantinople (modern Istanbul) on a map and explain its advantages.

learn: Emperor Justinian (ruled 527-565) reconquered lands and built the Hagia Sophia.
Justinian's Code organised Roman laws and influenced legal systems in Europe.
His wife Theodora was a powerful adviser.
lessons.try: Research the Hagia Sophia and describe its dome.

learn: In 1054, Christianity split into the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches.
Byzantine art featured mosaics and religious icons.
Byzantine scholars preserved Greek and Roman writings.
lessons.try: Design a small paper mosaic.

units.t: The Rise and Spread of Islam

learn: Islam began in the Arabian Peninsula in the 600s CE with the Prophet Muhammad.
Muslims believe in one God (Allah) and follow the Qur'an, their holy book.
The Five Pillars are faith, prayer, charity, fasting during Ramadan and pilgrimage to Mecca.
check: The holy book of Islam is the...
Fasting during Ramadan is one of the...
lessons.try: Make a chart of the Five Pillars of Islam.

learn: After Muhammad's death, caliphs led the Muslim community.
Islamic empires spread across Southwest Asia, North Africa and Spain.
Trade and conquest spread the Arabic language and Islam.
check: Islamic rule reached as far west as...
The language spread with Islam was...
lessons.try: Trace the expansion of the early caliphates on a map.

learn: Baghdad's House of Wisdom gathered scholars who translated and advanced knowledge.
Muslim scholars made advances in algebra, astronomy, medicine and optics.
Ibn Sina's medical book was used in Europe for centuries.
check: The House of Wisdom was in...
A subject advanced by Muslim scholars was...
lessons.try: Research one scholar from the Islamic Golden Age.

lessons.t: The Fall of Rome and the Early Middle Ages
learn: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.
Europe broke into small kingdoms. Charlemagne united much of western Europe around 800.
The Middle Ages lasted roughly from 500 to 1500.
check: The Western Roman Empire fell in...
lessons.try: Make a timeline of the Middle Ages.

learn: Feudalism was a system in which kings granted land to nobles in exchange for loyalty and military service.
Knights served lords; peasants and serfs worked the land.
The manor was a self-sufficient estate with a castle, village and fields.
check: At the top of the feudal pyramid was the...
lessons.try: Draw a feudal pyramid.

learn: The Catholic Church was the most powerful institution in medieval Europe.
Monasteries preserved learning by copying books by hand.
Gothic cathedrals had pointed arches and stained glass.
check: The most powerful institution was the...
lessons.try: Design a stained-glass window on paper.

learn: The Crusades (1096-1291) were religious wars over the Holy Land.
They increased trade and contact between Europe and Southwest Asia.
The Crusades also caused great suffering and lasting distrust.
check: The Crusades were fought over the...
An effect of the Crusades was more...
lessons.try: List effects of the Crusades on Europe.

learn: The Black Death, a plague, struck Europe in 1347-1351.
It was spread by fleas on rats and killed about one-third of Europe's people.
Labour shortages gave surviving peasants more bargaining power.
lessons.try: Explain how the plague changed society.

learn: In 1215, English nobles forced King John to sign Magna Carta.
It limited the king's power and said even rulers must follow the law.
It influenced later ideas of rights and constitutional government.
check: Magna Carta limited the power of the...
lessons.try: Discuss why limiting a ruler's power matters.

lessons.t: Ghana: The Gold and Salt Trade
learn: The Ghana Empire in West Africa grew rich from trading gold and salt.
Camel caravans crossed the Sahara Desert.
Ghana's kings taxed trade passing through.
lessons.try: Explain why salt was as valuable as gold.

learn: The Mali Empire grew powerful under Sundiata and Mansa Musa.
Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 was famous for its wealth.
Timbuktu became a centre of learning with libraries and universities.
lessons.try: Research Timbuktu's libraries.

learn: The Songhai Empire later controlled West African trade.
Great Zimbabwe built massive stone walls without mortar.
East African city-states like Kilwa traded across the Indian Ocean.
lessons.try: Compare Great Zimbabwe and Timbuktu.

learn: The Tang (618-907) and Song (960-1279) dynasties were golden ages in China.
Inventions included printing, gunpowder and the magnetic compass.
Civil service exams chose officials by merit.
check: Which was invented in Song China?
Civil service exams chose officials by...
lessons.try: Make a list of inventions from Tang and Song China.

learn: Genghis Khan united the Mongols in 1206 and built the largest land empire in history.
The Mongols protected trade on the Silk Road.
Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China and met Marco Polo.
lessons.try: Trace the Mongol Empire at its height.

learn: Japan's islands developed a unique culture influenced by China.
In feudal Japan, the shogun ruled with samurai warriors who followed the code of bushido.
Japanese culture produced haiku, tea ceremonies and Noh theatre.
check: The military ruler of Japan was the...
A Japanese poetry form is the...
lessons.try: Compare Japanese and European feudalism.

learn: The Renaissance ("rebirth") began in Italy in the 1300s.
Wealthy cities like Florence, funded by families like the Medici, supported artists.
Humanism focused on human potential and classical learning.
lessons.try: Explain why Italy was a good place for the Renaissance to begin.

learn: Leonardo da Vinci painted the "Mona Lisa" and filled notebooks with inventions.
Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Artists used perspective and realistic anatomy.
lessons.try: Study a page from Leonardo's notebooks.

learn: Johannes Gutenberg developed a movable-type printing press around 1450.
Books became cheaper and ideas spread quickly.
Literacy grew across Europe.
check: Who developed the movable-type printing press in Europe?
lessons.try: Make a stamp print of your initials.

learn: In 1517, Martin Luther posted 95 Theses criticising practices of the Catholic Church.
He argued that faith alone, not payments, leads to salvation.
The printing press spread his ideas quickly.
lessons.try: Explain how the printing press helped the Reformation.

learn: Protestant churches formed, including Lutheran, Calvinist and Anglican.
King Henry VIII founded the Church of England in 1534.
Europe divided along religious lines.
lessons.try: Make a chart of new Protestant churches and founders.

learn: The Catholic Church responded with reforms called the Counter-Reformation.
The Council of Trent clarified Catholic teachings.
The Jesuits founded schools and spread Catholicism.
check: The Catholic response is called the...
lessons.try: Compare the goals of the Reformation and Counter-Reformation.

units.t: The Age of Exploration and Its Consequences

learn: Europeans explored for gold, God and glory: wealth, spreading religion and fame.
New technology helped: the caravel ship, the astrolabe and better maps.
Prince Henry the Navigator supported Portuguese exploration.
check: The three Gs are gold, God and...
lessons.try: List the three Gs and give an example of each.

learn: Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in 1492.
Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to India in 1498.
Ferdinand Magellan's expedition first sailed around the world (1519-1522).
check: Who sailed around Africa to India?
The first round-the-world voyage was led by...
lessons.try: Trace three explorers' routes on a map.

lessons.t: The Columbian Exchange and Its Costs
learn: The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals and diseases between hemispheres.
Potatoes and maize went to Europe; horses and wheat came to the Americas.
Diseases like smallpox killed millions of Indigenous people, and the Atlantic slave trade forced millions of Africans into slavery.
check: Potatoes went from the Americas to...
lessons.try: Make a two-column chart of the Columbian Exchange.

learn: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed that Earth orbits the Sun (1543).
Galileo Galilei used a telescope to support this idea.
Isaac Newton described gravity and the laws of motion (1687).
check: Who proposed Earth orbits the Sun?
lessons.try: Explain how the scientific method changed how people learn about the world.

learn: The Enlightenment applied reason to government and society.
John Locke argued people have natural rights to life, liberty and property.
Montesquieu proposed separation of powers; Rousseau wrote about the social contract.
check: Locke argued for natural rights to life, liberty and...
lessons.try: Match each thinker to his idea.

learn: Enlightenment ideas inspired the American Revolution (1776) and French Revolution (1789).
The Declaration of Independence echoes Locke's ideas.
These ideas still shape democracies today.
check: The Declaration echoes the ideas of...
lessons.try: Find Locke's ideas in the Declaration of Independence.
